## Where we are going

- Say why project management became a mainstream skill, not a construction speciality.
- Apply the temporary-and-unique test — and find where it fails.
- Tell a project, a program and a portfolio apart.
- Describe the life cycle and how effort is distributed across it.
- Say what makes a project unsuitable for up-front planning.
- Separate the technical from the sociocultural, and master both.

# 1 · Why this is a mainstream skill

## Two numbers

**$2.5 trillion** — roughly a quarter of US gross national product — is spent on projects each year.

**93,000 → 686,000** — PMI membership, 2002 to 2021.

::: {.aside}
Larson & Gray, Ch. 1
:::

## The quieter observation

Most people who manage projects **never hold the title**.

Accountants running an audit · lawyers running a case · teachers coaching a debate team · a clinician organising a health event.

For them project management is not a job title but a **job requirement**.

## Which is the argument for you

With three to four career changes now typical, the skill travels better than almost anything else you will learn.

Project management fundamentals are **universal**.

# 2 · What a project is

## The definition

> A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.

**Temporary** — a definite beginning and end. Bounded, not brief.

**Unique** — not previously produced in this exact configuration.

## Five characteristics

| # | Characteristic |
|---|---|
| 1 | An established objective |
| 2 | A defined lifespan — beginning and end |
| 3 | Usually several departments and professions |
| 4 | Typically something not done before |
| 5 | Specific time, cost and performance requirements |

## The fifth one is the triple constraint

Time · cost · performance.

They impose a level of accountability ordinary work rarely carries.

Balancing the trade-offs among them — while still satisfying the customer — is the job.

## What a project is not

| Routine, repetitive | Project |
|---|---|
| Taking lecture notes | Writing the term paper |
| Posting invoices | Standing up a new billing system |
| Answering supply-chain queries | Building the dashboard they revealed a need for |
| Running weekly ceremonies | Migrating off the legacy repository |

## Why the distinction earns its keep

Resources consumed by daily operations are resources **not spent** on the work that carries the organisation forward.

Organisations that cannot tell the two apart starve the second.

## Where the test fails

- **A film production** — temporary and unique, but the studio makes one every year.
- **A software release train** — each release unique, the cadence operational.
- **A refinery shutdown** — recurring on a cycle, run as a project every time.

. . .

"Project vs. operation" is a decision about **which toolkit to apply** — not a fact about the world.

## Project · program · portfolio

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Project** | A temporary endeavour producing a unique output |
| **Program** | Related projects pursuing a common goal over an extended period |
| **Portfolio** | The set of projects and programs the organisation funds |

. . .

No dependencies between the components? It is a portfolio, and somebody chose a more impressive word.

# 3 · The project life cycle

## Four stages

| Stage | What comes out |
|---|---|
| **Defining** | Goals, specifications, tasks, responsibilities |
| **Planning** | Schedules, budgets, resources, risks, staffing |
| **Executing** | Status reports, changes, quality, forecasts |
| **Closing** | Training, documents, released resources, lessons learned |

## Effort is not evenly distributed

Executing dominates the effort curve.

Defining is short and cheap — **and is where the leverage is**.

. . .

The two stages most often skipped are defining and closing. Both are cheap. Both are where the money is made or lost.

## Closing is a real stage

Three activities, not one:

1. **Deliver** to the customer — training, transferred documents
2. **Redeploy** — equipment and people have to land somewhere
3. **Review** — assess performance *and* capture lessons

Skip the review and the organisation relearns the lesson at full price.

# 4 · When planning stops working

## Traditional PM assumes predictability

An engineer building a bridge draws on proven technology and established design principles.

**What** is to be accomplished and **how** are both well understood.

Not all projects enjoy that.

## Uncertainty has two axes

**Scope (what)** — how well is it known and stable?

**Technology (how)** — how proven is it?

. . .

Predictable → unpredictable → unknown. The further out you sit, the worse a fixed up-front plan performs.

## The cost of ignoring it

**$81 billion** — US spend on cancelled software projects, 1995 *(Standish Group)*

**> $2 trillion** — cost of poor software quality in the US, 2020 *(Krasner, 2022)*

::: {.aside}
The first figure is historical. The problem is not.
:::

## Rolling wave

An incremental, iterative process. Iterations of **one to four weeks**.

Each makes tangible progress — a requirement settled, a technical problem solved, a feature demonstrated — then is reviewed and feeds the next.

Each iteration **subsumes** the work of the last.

## Agile in one line

Active collaboration with customer representatives · small functional pieces · adapting to changing requirements.

Works best in **small teams of four to eight**.

## It is not either/or

Agile up front to establish specifications and requirements.

Traditional to plan, execute and close.

. . .

**Hybrid project management** — and it is the common case in practice, not a compromise.

# 5 · What is driving demand

## Compression of the product life cycle

High-tech product life cycles now average **six months to three years**. Thirty years ago, ten to fifteen years was unremarkable.

. . .

A **six-month delay** in a high-tech product can cost **a third** of its potential revenue share.

## Knowledge explosion

Building a road thirty years ago was comparatively simple.

Today: materials, specifications, codes, aesthetics, equipment, specialists.

Hard to find a new product without a microchip. Increasingly hard to find one without AI.

**Integration is the problem. Project management is the discipline that does it.**

## Triple bottom line

Planet · people · profit.

Sustainability moved from public relations to a **design constraint** — it shows up in project objectives and techniques.

On construction projects, LEED certification is now routinely an objective in its own right.

## Small projects, big problems

Small projects carry the **same or more risk** than large ones.

Because each inefficiency is small and unmeasured, it is invisible.

In aggregate the losses are substantial — and sit outside the accounting system.

. . .

The problem is organisational: prioritising across a portfolio. That is Week 2.

# 6 · The socio-technical dimension

## Two dimensions, different in kind

| Technical | Sociocultural |
|---|---|
| Scope · WBS | Leadership |
| Schedules | Problem solving |
| Resource allocation | Teamwork · negotiation |
| Baseline budgets | Politics |
| Status reports | Customer expectations |

## The technical dimension is the orderly one

Scope statements link the project to the customer.

The WBS is the **database** connecting every level of the organisation to every deliverable, down to the tasks in a work package.

Integrated linkages mean any change is documented and **traceable to its source**.

## The sociocultural dimension is not orderly

Messy, often contradictory, paradoxical.

Shape a culture that sustains teamwork and motivation · spot problems before they threaten the work · steer back when — not if — things depart from plan.

Build a cooperative network among stakeholders with genuinely **different standards, commitments and perspectives**.

## Master both

Competence in one does not compensate for weakness in the other.

The failure modes look nothing alike.

# 7 · Where generative AI enters

## Across the process groups

| Group | Applied to |
|---|---|
| **Initiating** | Idea generation · stakeholder content · requirements |
| **Planning** | Plan drafting · risk scenarios · scenario planning |
| **Executing** | Content · code generation · dynamic reporting |
| **Monitoring** | Risk narratives · feedback loops · predictive models |
| **Closing** | Automated summary reports |

## Read that table carefully

Every row describes a **generated artefact**.

A generated artefact is a claim, not a result.

. . .

A model produces a plausible, well-formatted WBS in nine seconds and quietly omits a stakeholder — because it does not know who is in your room.

## The rule for this course

**The check is graded, not the output.**

Generate the artifact with a model — then write the code that checks it.
